Emergent larval measurements of Humpback chub (Gila cypha) during incubation at 21.5 °C [T = 21.5 °C] show that the age at hatch averages approximately 5.2 days , based on reported ranges between 102 and 149 hours divided across a 24-hour reference. In the Colorado River system, where this endemic cyprinid persists, the small size at eclosion is notable: newly emerged prolarvae measure a standard length of 0.7 cm [Lb = 0.7 cm], an average derived from hatch-length estimates of 6.7 to 7.4 millimeters converted to centimeters. The wet weight at birth, measured at hatch rather than at yolk-sac resorption, averages 0.0035 grams [Wwb = 0.0035 grams], representing the midpoint of values spanning 2.8 to 4.2 milligrams. These early-life metrics situate G. cypha among the smaller-bodied cyprinids at the onset of exogenous feeding, a trait that may influence larval drift distance and vulnerability to predation during the critical transition to the planktonic phase.

Adult Humpback chub attain a maximum total length of 41 centimeters [Li = 41 centimeters], a figure corresponding to the largest females recorded in the Colorado River basin. This ultimate total length exceeds typical male values, which FishBase reports near 38 centimeters, reflecting pronounced sexual size dimorphism in this species. The asymptotic wet weight, calculated from length-mass regressions for the basin, reaches 716 grams [Wwi = 716 grams], a value derived from the equation 0.00813 times the cube of total length. A female of 40.6 centimeters total length, near the upper end of the adult size range, produces an estimated annual reproductive output of about 5445 eggs per year [Ri = about 5445 eggs per year], equivalent to an ultimate reproductive rate of about 14.92 eggs per day  at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. Under the average thermal regime of the mainstem Colorado River at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], this annual fecundity likely translates to multiple spawning events, though the precise number of clutches per year remains uncertain and probably depends on flow conditions and thermal heterogeneity.

Field studies in the Grand Canyon indicate that the Humpback chub lifespan extends to approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years], with the oldest documented individuals reaching this age in the mainstem Colorado River under natural thermal regimes averaging 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This maximum longevity is relatively modest for a cyprinid of this body size, especially compared to large-bodied minnows from cooler, more stable habitats in the upper Colorado basin. In contrast, captive-held individuals in controlled environments may persist beyond this period, though wild senescence appears to constrain populations. The completion of the life cycle within roughly half a decade places G. cypha among the shorter-lived large-river cyprinids, a life history strategy that may buffer against environmental stochasticity through rapid population turnover when conditions favor recruitment. Records from long-term monitoring programs show that the oldest fish captured in mark-recapture efforts are consistently near this upper bound, suggesting that mortality increases sharply after the fourth year in the wild.

Sexual maturity in Humpback chub occurs after an extended juvenile phase, with individuals reaching puberty at approximately 730 days since birth [tp = approximately 730 days since birth], a duration that corresponds to two full growing seasons under the thermal conditions of the Colorado River, which maintains an average temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This time since birth at puberty is consistent with field observations that adults are at least two to three years old when first captured in spawning condition. The prolonged juvenile stage, lasting about 24 months, allows for the accumulation of sufficient somatic mass and lipid stores necessary for the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and spawning migration. Gonadal recrudescence in this species is triggered by a combination of photoperiod cues and temperature thresholds, with mature oocytes developing over several months before the spring spawning window. This age at puberty represents a relatively late onset of reproduction compared to smaller-bodied Colorado River cyprinids, reflecting the larger body size and longer generation time characteristic of G. cypha within the endemic fish assemblage.

When compared to other large-bodied cyprinids endemic to the Colorado River, the growth trajectory of Humpback chub is characterized by a relatively rapid early phase followed by a gradual approach to asymptotic size. The standard length at birth of 0.7 cm [Lb = 0.7 cm] is comparable to that of the closely related bonytail (Gila elegans), though the ultimate total length of 41 cm [Li = 41 cm] exceeds that species' typical maximum. The wet weight at hatch of 0.0035 grams [Wwb = 0.0035 grams] reflects a modest maternal investment per offspring that is offset by high fecundity and potentially compensatory growth in productive floodplain habitats. The age at hatch of approximately 5.2 days  at 21.5 °C [T = 21.5 °C] is relatively brief for a cyprinid egg of this size, a trait that may reduce egg mortality from sedimentation and siltation in turbid river environments. These early life-stage parameters, combined with an adult life span of approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] and puberty at 730 days since birth [tp = 730 days since birth], define a life history that balances rapid early development against a moderate reproductive window.
